seoDescription: Master the essential Capacitor workflow for building and deploying iOS and Android applications from your web project. This guide walks through initializing Capacitor in an Ionic application, configuring `capacitor.config.json`, and managing the web assets directory (`www`). Learn to add native platforms, build your web code, and synchronize assets and plugins using key commands like `ionic cap add`, `copy`, `update`, and `sync`.

chapters.title: Enabling Capacitor in an Ionic Project
chapters.description: Learn how to initialize Capacitor in a new or existing Ionic application using a single command.

chapters.title: Understanding capacitor.config.json
chapters.description: This chapter explains the key properties in the `capacitor.config.json` file, including `appId` and `webDir`.

chapters.title: Building Your Web Assets
chapters.description: See how to generate the web directory (`www` folder) using the `ionic build` command, a crucial step before syncing with native platforms.

chapters.title: Adding Native iOS & Android Platforms
chapters.description: This chapter covers adding the native iOS and Android projects to your Capacitor application using the `ionic cap add` command.

chapters.title: Opening Projects in Xcode & Android Studio
chapters.description: Discover Capacitor's native-centric approach by using `ionic cap open` to manage, run, and debug your application in Xcode and Android Studio.

chapters.title: The Core Development Loop: Syncing Web Code
chapters.description: Follow the typical development cycle of modifying web code, rebuilding, and then copying the updated assets to your native projects with `ionic cap copy`.

chapters.title: Adding & Syncing Cordova Plugins
chapters.description: Learn how to install Cordova plugins using `npm` and then synchronize them with your native projects using the `ionic cap update` command.

chapters.title: Using `ionic cap sync` for a Combined Workflow
chapters.description: Simplify your workflow by using the `ionic cap sync` command, which combines copying web assets and updating native plugins in a single step.

chapters.title: Summary and Next Steps
chapters.description: A final recap of the general Capacitor workflow and a look at what topics, like app signing and resources, are involved in the final build process.

summary:
## Initial Capacitor Setup

- Enable Capacitor in an existing Ionic project with `ionic integrations enable capacitor`.
- For non-Ionic projects, follow the standard Capacitor documentation for setup.
- The `capacitor.config.json` file is created automatically and contains key settings:
    - **`appId`**: The unique bundle ID for your application (e.g., `com.company.appname`).
    - **`webDir`**: The folder containing your built web assets. For Ionic, this is typically `www`.

## The Build & Sync Workflow

1.  **Build your web app**: Before syncing, you must build your web code.
    - For Ionic: `ionic build` (or `ionic build --prod` for production).
    - This creates the directory specified in `webDir` (e.g., `www`).
2.  **Add native platforms**: Create the native project folders.
    - `ionic cap add ios`
    - `ionic cap add android`
3.  **Sync your changes**: After making changes to your web code or plugins, sync them to the native projects.
    - **Sync web assets**: `ionic cap copy`
    - **Sync native plugins**: `ionic cap update`
    - **Sync everything**: `ionic cap sync` (combines `copy` and `update`).

> [!NOTE]
> For non-Ionic projects, use the `npx cap <command>` syntax (e.g., `npx cap sync`) for all Capacitor CLI operations.

## Working with Native Projects

- Capacitor delegates running, debugging, and building to the native IDEs (Xcode and Android Studio).
- Open a native project in its IDE using the `open` command:
    - `ionic cap open ios` (opens Xcode)
    - `ionic cap open android` (opens Android Studio)
- Once open, you can run the app on an emulator/device, use native debugging tools, and perform final builds for app store submission.

## Managing Plugins

- Capacitor is compatible with most Cordova plugins.
- **Installation**: Install Cordova plugins using `npm`, not the Cordova CLI.
    - `npm install cordova-plugin-example`

> [!IMPORTANT]
> After installing or removing a plugin, you **must** run `ionic cap update` or `ionic cap sync` for the changes to be reflected in your native iOS and Android projects.
transcription:
## Enabling Capacitor in an Ionic Project

In this video, we're going to look at how to use Capacitor. We have an Ionic application, but it's going to be looking at the general workflow. We're going to see what it looks like when you're developing an application using Capacitor. So most of what I'm going to be talking about won't be specific to Ionic. We're going to use the Ionic/Capacitor commands, but you could just as easily use this information for a general Capacitor app built with anything.

So what I have on screen now is just an Ionic application that I've just generated. It's just a standard blank application. And what we're going to do is first get Capacitor enabled in here and then work through some of the commands. As I'm currently working with the beta of Ionic 4, in the future, Capacitor integration will probably be enabled by default, or you'll have an option to do that when you generate the project. But for now, we can just run the `ionic integrations` command to get that enabled.

So if you just come into your project and run `ionic integrations enable capacitor`, that's going to set up that Capacitor integration for you. So it's going to handle, as you can see here, installing the Capacitor core library for you. And this is going to handle all the setup that you need done. If you weren't using Ionic, obviously you're not going to be able to use that `ionic integrations` command, in which case, just follow the normal setup in the Capacitor documentation.

## Understanding capacitor.config.json

Okay, so now that that's finished generating, if you come back into the project over here, you'll see we have this `capacitor.config.json` file. So if we take a look, it's just a simple configuration file here. There's not really too much you need to worry about doing in this file. It is important to take note of the `appId`, and this is the bundle ID that's going to be used if you build this as an iOS application or an Android application. So you'll probably want to change this to something specific to you or your company or your application. For this, you usually use a reverse domain style name, so it might be something like `com.yourcompany.yourproject`.

The other important thing here is the `webDir` or the web directory. And so this is just the folder that you're telling Capacitor to pull in the web assets from. Capacitor is very similar to Cordova in that it's just running web code inside of a webview in a native application. And so Capacitor will handle creating the native application for you, and then it's just looking here to see, 'Well, where do you want us to pull in the web code from?'

And so this is the built output of your Ionic application. So when you're building with Capacitor, it's going to look for this `www` folder on your project here, and then it's going to pull in the web assets from there. And so if we look in the folder structure here now, you'll see that a `www` folder isn't anywhere to be seen.

## Building Your Web Assets

That's because that folder is only created after we do a build of our application. So to do that, all we need to do is run the `ionic build` command. Or if you're creating your production, your final application, you'll want to run `ionic build --prod` to create a production build. But we'll just do a development build for now. So you run `ionic build`, and that's going to generate that `www` folder for you.

And again, if you're not using Ionic, obviously you're not going to be able to use the `ionic build` command. In that case, just do whatever it is you need to do to build your application to get your sort of final built output, your optimized output. And then whatever folder you're outputting that final code to, just set that as the web directory or just create that directory as `www` in your project.

And now that `ionic build` command is finished, we can see we have that `www` folder now, and that contains all of the build output for the application. And so everything inside of here is actually what we'll be running. And say, if you build your iOS application, this is what code is going to be run. All the rest of your project is never included in that native application. It's just this `www` folder.

## Adding Native iOS & Android Platforms

Now that we have Capacitor set up, we've got our web directory created here with our built output, we can tell Capacitor to copy that over to the native project and then we can open it in Xcode or Android studio to do a build. So before we can actually use iOS or the Android platform, we need to add those as platforms in our project.

So to do that, let's say if we want to add the iOS platform, we'll just run `ionic cap add iOS`. And that's going to handle adding the iOS platform for us. And if we just look at some of the messages that popped up here, you can see that it says it's copying web assets from the `www` folder to `ios/public`. It's doing a bunch of other stuff in here as well. It hasn't found any plugins, so nothing is being included there. And so since we already have that `www` folder created, it's automatically copying our web assets for us, but we're going to talk about how to do that manually afterwards as well.

And so whilst we're here, let's also add the Android platform. So you just would be able to run `ionic cap add Android`. And so I'm using the `ionic cap` command here, which is just a shortcut for using the Capacitor commands in an Ionic application. If you're not using Ionic, again, obviously you can't use `ionic cap`, but you could just use the standard `npx cap` command instead. But aside from that, it's basically you'll be running the same commands, just you know, you won't be using `ionic cap`.

Okay, so now the Android platform has been added as well. Again, you can see it's copying the web assets from `www` to the Android platform. And again, there haven't been any plugins found because there's no plugins installed in this project. But we now have both the iOS platform and the Android platform set up.

## Opening Projects in Xcode & Android Studio

Unlike something like Cordova, where a lot of the work happens in the command line, if you wanted to run your application, for example, you'd run it through here. With Capacitor, there's more focus on using, I guess, the default native tools, so using Xcode and Android Studio. Basically, most of what Capacitor does is it just sets up your native project and it handles copying the assets from your project, so the web assets or any plugins, and handles setting those up in the native project.

But if we want to, say, run a test build, we will just open that up in Xcode or Android Studio. So let's say for example, I want to run my iOS application on the device, I could just run `ionic cap open iOS`. That's going to open my project inside of Xcode. And so once you're inside of Xcode, you'll be able to really do anything with the native project that you could with any native project. You don't need to understand any of that. There's very little you actually have to do in Xcode, although you can do quite a bit. But for a lot of people, that's just going to be you're going to want to run your application on a device, you're going to want to do the final build of the application and get it signed. But for the most part, you're just going to be opening up your application in Xcode using `ionic cap open iOS` or `npx cap open iOS` if you're not using Ionic. And once you're in here, you'll just be able to select what you want to run the application on. You could use one of the emulators, or if you've got your device connected by USB, if you just select that in here, hit play, and that's going to run that on your device and you'll be able to debug it or do whatever you want with it.

And it's the same for the Android platform. If we run `ionic cap open Android`, that's just going to open up a native Android project inside of Android Studio. And so when you open that, it's going to do all the Gradle sync stuff it does with just normal Android projects. But again, if you want to run this application on your device, you're just going to plug it in by USB or you can use one of the emulators and just click this play button here, and it's going to let you select where you want to run the application. And again, when it comes to doing the final build of your application, you can also use Android Studio to handle that.

## The Core Development Loop: Syncing Web Code

So what will typically happen with your development workflow here is that for the most part, you're going to be working inside of your standard Ionic application or whatever web application you're building. You do most of the work in here, but obviously at some point, we need to get that code over into our native application. And so anytime that you make a change to any of the web code—if you're changing your templates or your TypeScript files, you're adding images in your assets folder, basically any change you're making to the actual web code of the Ionic application—you need to use the `npx cap copy` or `ionic cap copy` command to perform this step to copy the web assets from `www` to the native projects.

You can just run `ionic cap copy`. And you can see that's running the Capacitor copy command, and that's going to copy the web assets from the `www` folder to the native Android project and to the native iOS project. And remember, you actually have to do a build before that works. If you make any changes in here, it's not going to be reflected in the actual output of your application until you run the build command, because that's what's being copied over.

And the other thing you need to keep in mind is if you're using native plugins, because they also need to be copied over to the native project.

## Adding & Syncing Cordova Plugins

I've just got up an example native plugin here from Ionic Native, the Crop plugin. I basically just chose this one at random. And so if you look at the installation steps here, it says to run `ionic cordova plugin add cordova-plugin-crop`. So with Capacitor, you can still use most Cordova plugins, but you won't use the `cordova plugin add` command to add those. Instead, you just run it as a standard `npm install` command. So in this case, I'd run `npm install cordova-plugin-crop`. So let's just do that now. Hit enter to save that into our project or to install into the project.

And if you like, you can still use the Ionic Native library to manage these plugins as well in your application if you like using the Ionic Native API. But also do keep in mind that Capacitor also has its own inbuilt API that you can use as well. But in this particular instance, Capacitor doesn't have its own crop API, so you could install this plugin, you could just use the standard Cordova syntax to use it, or if there is an Ionic Native wrapper available, you can install that and use that as well.

Okay, so that plugin is finished installing now, but at this point in time, it's not actually set up in our native project. So just like with the `ionic cap copy` command that we use to copy the web assets over, if we make any changes to the plugins, we'll need to run `ionic cap update`. And you can see here it says it found one Cordova plugin for Android and it's copied that over. And it also found a Cordova plugin for iOS, which is the crop plugin that we just installed. And now that we've run that command, that's been successfully copied over to our native projects. So you can use those two commands separately. You can use `ionic cap copy` and `ionic cap update` to copy those things over separately.

## Using `ionic cap sync` for a Combined Workflow

You can also just run the `ionic cap sync` command, and that is going to both copy the web assets and it's going to check for any native plugins and copy those as well. So if you just want to do both things in one hit, run `ionic cap sync`. Or if you just want to remember the one thing, you can just run this all the time if you want.

## Summary and Next Steps

Okay, so those basic steps that I've gone through in this video is most of what you'll need to know to work with Capacitor. Really, the only time you're going to need to know anything more than what we've discussed is when you're doing the final build of your application and you're trying to set up signing and the app resources like the icons and the splash screen and that kind of thing. But the general workflow is basically what I've shown you here. You just mostly work inside of your standard Ionic application or whatever you're using. When you're ready to run and test that on a device, you just copy over the assets to the native project and you run it through Xcode or Android Studio.

Okay, so I hope you enjoyed this video. If you want to check out my book which covers Capacitor in a lot of depth, there's a link to that in the description, as well as my Twitter and stuff like that if you want to follow me on social media. Thanks for watching, and I'll see you in the next one.
